title: A modern dishwasher uses about ten litres of water for a full load, twelve pl…
caption:
A modern dishwasher uses about ten litres of water for a full load, twelve place settings, and heats it to sixty degrees. A person washing the same dishes by hand under a running tap uses somewhere between forty and a hundred, and the studies that have measured people at real sinks put the average nearer the top. The machine wins by a factor of four to ten.

It wins because it washes the same small volume over and over: a pump sprays a few litres round the cabinet for an hour, the water is filtered and sprayed again, and only at the end is it drained and replaced. A tap does not recycle. It runs at six to ten litres a minute into a sink whose water goes straight to the drain.

Washing up in a bowl, with the tap off, is a different story: fifteen or twenty litres, close to the machine, if the rinse is done in a second bowl rather than under the tap. The myth is that the machine is the wasteful option. The waste, in the kitchen as in the bathroom, is the running tap.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#watermyths #drinkingwater #water #thirstyplanet

title: Nairobi needs about 800,000 cubic metres of water a day and gets about 500,00…
caption:
Nairobi needs about 800,000 cubic metres of water a day and gets about 500,000. The difference is managed by rota: every district of the city has its water turned off for part of every week, and has had since 2017, when a drought emptied the Ndakaini dam and the utility decided the schedule was permanent. Of the 500,000 that enter the pipes, close to half leak out or are never paid for.

The people who pay most are the people with no pipe. In Kibera and Mathare, the informal settlements that hold a third of the city, water comes from kiosks and vendors at a few shillings a jerry can, which works out at five to ten times what a household in a wealthy suburb pays per litre for water from its own tap, and it runs out when the rota turns the mains off upstream.

The fix, twenty years in the planning, is a tunnel under the Aberdare hills that brings three rivers into the city's dam. It opened, in stages, from 2022. It adds about a quarter to the supply, and the city grows by about that much each decade.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#watercrisis #watersecurity #water #thirstyplanet

title: In 1854 a doctor in London named John Snow mapped the deaths in a cholera out…
caption:
In 1854 a doctor in London named John Snow mapped the deaths in a cholera outbreak in Soho and found them clustered around one public pump on Broad Street. He persuaded the parish to take the handle off. The outbreak, already fading, ended, and the idea that a disease could travel in water rather than in bad air had its first piece of evidence. The pump's well, it turned out, was a metre from a leaking cesspit.

Thirty years later the bacterium was identified, and within a generation every city that could afford it had built what London built after its Great Stink: sewers to take the waste away and filtered, later chlorinated, water to bring the supply in. Cholera left those cities and has never come back.

It kills tens of thousands a year today, in Yemen, Haiti, Sudan, the Congo and the camps of every war and flood, where the supply is a river that the sewage runs into. It is curable with a bag of salt and sugar in clean water, and it is prevented with a treatment plant and a sewer, which is the whole of this site in one disease.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#watertreatment #wastewater #water #thirstyplanet

title: A kilogram of sunflower oil carries about 6,800 litres of water. The seed car…
caption:
A kilogram of sunflower oil carries about 6,800 litres of water. The seed carries about 3,400, and the oil is twice that because a kilogram of seed gives less than half a kilogram of oil, and the water follows the oil. Olive oil is 14,500. Rapeseed is 4,300. Palm oil is about 5,000, and the argument about palm oil is about land, not water.

Almost all of the sunflower's water is rain. The crop grows on the steppe of Ukraine and southern Russia, on the plains of Argentina and in the dry summers of southern Europe, with a tap root that goes two metres down and finds water that a shallower crop misses. It is rarely irrigated and it is one of the least thirsty oils on this site, in the water that anyone else could have had.

The war in Ukraine in 2022 took half the world's sunflower oil exports off the market in a month and put rationing signs on supermarket shelves in Europe. The water was never the problem. The port was.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

title: About half the nitrogen in the protein of every person alive passed through a…
caption:
About half the nitrogen in the protein of every person alive passed through an ammonia plant. The Haber Bosch process takes hydrogen, mostly from natural gas, and nitrogen from the air, and joins them at high pressure into ammonia, which becomes urea, ammonium nitrate and the other fertilisers that doubled the world's food in a century. The world makes about 180 million tonnes of it a year.

Water is in the recipe. The hydrogen comes from splitting methane with steam, and about half of the hydrogen atoms in the ammonia came from water: roughly a tonne of water, as an ingredient, in every tonne of ammonia. The plant then needs many tonnes more to carry away the heat, which is why every ammonia plant is on a river, a coast or a large cooling tower.

The water that matters more is at the other end. Ammonia becomes fertiliser, fertiliser becomes nitrate, and nitrate is in the wells and rivers of every farming region on Earth, which is the story the nitrate article on this site tells. The plant's water is a footnote to the fertiliser's.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#waterfootprint #industrialwater #water #thirstyplanet

title: A filter jug does one thing well: it takes the chlorine out of tap water and …
caption:
A filter jug does one thing well: it takes the chlorine out of tap water and with it the taste and smell that people dislike. It also takes out some of the hardness, a little lead and copper if the pipes are shedding them, and not much else. It does not remove nitrate, fluoride, most pesticides, PFAS, or bacteria and viruses, and the tests that back the claims on the box are tests of taste, not of safety.

The water that comes out of the jug can be less safe than the water that went in. The chlorine that the cartridge removes is what stops bacteria growing in the water, and the carbon it removes it with is a warm, wet, nutrient rich surface on which bacteria grow very well. Studies of jugs in ordinary kitchens have found bacterial counts in the filtered water many times those in the tap, especially after the four weeks the cartridge is supposed to last.

If the tap water meets the standard, the jug makes it taste better and that is all. If it does not, the jug is the wrong filter for almost every reason it might fail.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

title: Istanbul sits on the Bosphorus with the Black Sea at one end and the Marmara …
caption:
Istanbul sits on the Bosphorus with the Black Sea at one end and the Marmara at the other, and it is short of water. In January 2021 its reservoirs fell to a fifth, the lowest in fifteen years, and the utility said publicly that the city had about forty five days of supply left. Prayers for rain were said in the mosques. Then it rained, and the crisis passed, and the reason for it did not.

The reason is growth. Istanbul had a million people in 1950 and has sixteen million now, and it has outgrown every reservoir built for it: Terkos in the 1880s, Ömerli in the 1970s, a pipe from the Melen river two hundred kilometres to the east in the 2010s. Each was the answer for a decade. The city's rain falls mostly in winter, its reservoirs are shallow and its catchments are being built over, and in a dry winter the arithmetic runs out. Each reservoir was the answer for a decade, and each decade the city grew past it.

The Melen dam, which was meant to finish the job, cracked during construction and was years late. It is the city's insurance and it is not yet fully in place.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#watercrisis #watersecurity #water #thirstyplanet

title: Most cities older than a century carry rain and sewage in the same pipe. The …
caption:
Most cities older than a century carry rain and sewage in the same pipe. The Victorian engineers who built the sewers had one pipe to lay and put everything in it, and they built overflows along it so that when a storm filled the pipe faster than the works could take it, the excess would go into the river rather than back up into the streets. The overflows still work. In England in 2023 they spilled for 3.6 million hours.

What comes out is rainwater mixed with sewage, diluted but untreated, and for a hundred years nobody counted it, because nobody was watching. From 2016 the overflows in England were fitted with monitors, by 2023 nearly all of them, and the count that resulted turned a plumbing detail into the largest environmental argument in the country.

The fix is storage: tanks and tunnels that hold the storm flow until the works can treat it. London's answer is a tunnel twenty five kilometres long under the Thames that cost about five billion pounds and opened in 2025. Every old city has the same sewers and most have not yet built the tunnel.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#watertreatment #wastewater #water #thirstyplanet

title: An outdoor cannabis plant in a California summer uses about twenty two litres…
caption:
An outdoor cannabis plant in a California summer uses about twenty two litres of water a day, which is about twice what a grapevine on the same hillside takes. Over a season of a hundred and fifty days that is three thousand litres or more a plant, and a plant gives about half a kilogram to a kilogram of dried flower. Per kilogram the number is in the thousands of litres, which puts cannabis near beef and far above any vegetable, and per crop the number is tiny, because the crop is tiny.

The problem was never the total. It was where and when. Before legalisation the grows were in the forested hills of northern California, in the catchments of small streams that run low in summer, and the water was pumped straight out of them in August, when the salmon needed it most. A study of four watersheds in 2015 found grows taking more than the streams' entire summer flow.

Indoor growing uses less water and vastly more electricity: about one percent of the electricity in the United States goes to growing cannabis under lights. Legalisation brought permits, meters and tanks, and it moved the crop to farmland with rights to the water it uses.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#waterfootprint #hiddenwater #water #thirstyplanet

title: One egg carries about 196 litres of water, and the hen drank almost none of it.
caption:
One egg carries about 196 litres of water, and the hen drank almost none of it.

A laying hen eats around 110 grams of feed a day, mostly maize and soybean meal, and lays an egg most days. Grow all that grain, divide its water by the eggs, and an egg comes to about 3,300 litres per kilo, or 196 litres for a 60 gram egg, by the Water Footprint Network's method. Her own drinking water is a few percent of that.

The number that makes the egg interesting is the one per gram of protein. Eggs need about 29 litres for a gram of protein, close to milk, a third of pork and a quarter of beef. Among animal foods, the egg is one of the most efficient there is, and about four fifths of its water is rain on a field of grain.

As always, the field decides the rest. Maize irrigated in a dry region and soy grown on rain in Brazil carry very different water, and the carton does not say which the hen ate.

The long version, with the sources, is on thirstyplanet.media. Link in bio.

#waterfootprint #hiddenwater #water #thirstyplanet

title: Pick up a bottle of mineral water and look for the small print, usually somew…
caption:
Pick up a bottle of mineral water and look for the small print, usually somewhere near the bottom. There will be a line saying dry residue at 180 degrees, followed by a number. That number is TDS, total dissolved solids, and it is the single most useful measurement in the water business.

It is everything dissolved into the water: salt, calcium, magnesium, whatever the water met on its way through the ground. Rainwater has almost none. Tap water usually runs a few hundred milligrams per litre. Seawater is around thirty five thousand.

Two things follow from that, and they are both slightly funny. The first is that this number is what water tastes like. Water with nothing dissolved in it tastes flat and strange, which is why distilled water is unpleasant to drink and why bottled water brands advertise their minerals rather than hiding them. Some sparkling mineral waters carry more than a thousand milligrams per litre and charge a premium for it, while in the next aisle people buy filters designed to take exactly that out.

The second is that dissolved is a genuinely hard problem. A filter catches things by being too small to let them through, and dissolved salt has come apart into pieces far smaller than that. You cannot strain it, you cannot settle it, and bacteria will not eat it. The only ways out are to push the water through a membrane at about seventy times atmospheric pressure, boil it away, or trade the salt onto a resin. All of them cost energy, which is why salt is the wall that every water recycling project eventually hits.

The kettle limescale, the label on the bottle, the brine at the end of the pipe. Same number, three disguises.

#water #TDS #watertreatment #desalination #thirstyplanet #thewateryoucantsee

title: This account has spent a lot of posts arguing that a big water number is not …
caption:
This account has spent a lot of posts arguing that a big water number is not automatically bad news. Chocolate drinks tropical rain. Coffee mostly does too. Eggs turn out to be one of the better deals in the fridge. The avocado is where that argument stops.

The difference is not the size of the number, it is where the water comes from. Cocoa trees stand in some of the wettest places on Earth and drink what falls on them. Avocados prefer dry Mediterranean climates, which means Chile, Spain, Mexico, California, and in those places the water arrives through a pipe. Someone pumped it out of a river or a well, and it was not going to be available for anything else.

Petorca in Chile is the case everyone in the water world knows. It is a fruit growing province where plantations expanded fast, rivers ran low, and residents ended up receiving drinking water by tanker truck while orchards nearby stayed green. That is not a footprint calculation, it is a truck in a village.

None of which means avocados are forbidden. It means avocados are the fruit where origin actually matters, and the sticker on the skin tells you more about water than any number on a chart does.

You may see 320 litres per avocado quoted elsewhere rather than 400. Both come from the same underlying research, they just assume different sized fruit.

Sources: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011); reporting on Petorca, Chile.

#avocado #food #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet #thewateryoucantsee

title: Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winem…
caption:
Almost every farmer on Earth is trying to get more water to their crop. Winemakers are the strange exception. They spend their careers trying to make the plant a little thirsty.

A vine with plenty of water grows big, watery grapes and lots of leaves. A vine that has to work sends its roots down and produces small grapes with concentrated flavour, which is what ends up tasting like something. Growers call the technique deficit irrigation, and in parts of Europe the rules go further: several famous appellations simply forbid irrigation, on the grounds that a vineyard that needs watering is planted in the wrong place.

All of which makes the number a little awkward. A glass of wine still carries about 109 litres of water, and per litre wine costs roughly three times what beer does. Grapes are not especially thirsty, there just are not many of them per bottle, and the vine drinks rain all season either way.

The part worth watching is what heat is doing to those old rules. Regions that built their identity on never irrigating are now facing summers their vines were not planted for, and some of those bans have quietly started to bend. A tradition built around scarcity is running into actual scarcity.

Numbers in the slides.

Source: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011).

#wine #food #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet #thewateryoucantsee

title: A wastewater plant does not make dirt disappear. Nothing does. What a plant a…
caption:
A wastewater plant does not make dirt disappear. Nothing does. What a plant actually does is sort: clean water goes out one way, and everything that was in it gets gathered into a single heap. That heap has a name, sludge, and it is the part of the industry nobody puts on the brochure.

Two things about it surprise people. The first is that sludge is almost entirely water, about 99% of it at the start. The plant then spends enormous effort squeezing that down to a cake that is roughly a quarter solids and still feels damp. So a good deal of the machinery in a treatment works exists to take water out of something that was just taken out of water. The second is the bill. Handling sludge can eat up to half of a plant's running costs. The clean water gets the credit, the leftovers get the budget.

There is a genuinely good story in here too. Left in a sealed tank at roughly body temperature for three weeks, bacteria digest the pile without oxygen and give off biogas, which plants burn for heat and power. And what remains is full of nitrogen and phosphorus, which is exactly what farmland wants. Phosphorus in particular is mined from rock in a handful of countries and is not unlimited, so recovering it from sewage is not a hippie idea, it is arithmetic.

The complication is that everything anyone pours down a drain ends up in the same heap. Metals, microplastics, and the forever chemicals known as PFAS. In 2022 Maine banned spreading treated sludge on farmland because of them, and other places are reviewing the same question. So the pile is simultaneously a fertiliser and a puzzle, which is roughly where the industry currently stands.

Next time you pass a treatment works and see the round tanks with domed lids, those are the digesters. Something is having dinner in there.

#water #wastewater #sludge #biosolids #thirstyplanet #thewateryoucantsee

title: Cook one dinner and look at the sink afterwards. The colander, the pans, the …
caption:
Cook one dinner and look at the sink afterwards. The colander, the pans, the board covered in potato peel, the water going brown in the bowl. That is a food factory, except it never stops and it handles tonnes an hour.

Food and beverage is a bigger industry than most people picture. Dairies, breweries, bottling plants, bakeries, meat plants, canneries, sugar mills. In Europe it is the largest manufacturing sector there is, measured by turnover or by jobs, and one of the heaviest industrial users of water anywhere.

Here is the strange part: most of that water never touches the food. Somewhere between half and two thirds of it goes on cleaning the equipment. A crisp factory receives potatoes still wearing the field, so the first thing that happens is a wash. Then steam peeling, then slicing, then another rinse to take off the loose starch. Then frying, cooling, and at the end of the shift the whole line gets washed down. A bottling plant rinses every bottle. A dairy pushes hot water and detergent through its own pipework between every batch, a routine called cleaning in place, and in some plants that cleaning uses more water than the milk it processed. A one litre bottle of soft drink typically takes about two litres to produce, and most of that second litre went on the line, not the bottle.

The constraint that makes this hard: nobody can simply wash less. When the product is food, hygiene is not a place to economise. So the industry got clever in another direction, and my favourite trick is the simplest one. Rinse water is used in order, cleanest job first, dirtiest job last, so the water that gave a clean tank its final rinse goes on to wash the soil off the incoming potatoes. 

And the water leaving the far end is full of sugar, starch and milk, which bacteria are delighted to eat. Feed it into a sealed tank with no oxygen and it becomes biogas the factory burns in its own boilers. The washing up ends up heating the kitchen.

Sources: FoodDrinkEurope; published facility water studies; potato processing and cleaning in place practice; typical effluent characterisation.

#food #beverage #wastewater #biogas #thirstyplanet #thewateryoucantsee

title: Every office email footer used to beg the same thing: please consider the env…
caption:
Every office email footer used to beg the same thing: please consider the environment before printing. Here's what that request was actually worth: about 10 litres of water per sheet.

Most of it went through a tree. A plantation pine or eucalyptus drinks rain for years before it becomes pulp, and that patience is what the sheet inherits. The mill's share used to be enormous too, but this is one of industry's quiet success stories. A modern paper mill runs its water in loops and uses about a tenth of what mills used decades ago. The machines improved. The tree still takes its time.

The everyday scale is what makes paper interesting. One sheet is nothing. A ream is 5,000 litres. An office printer that runs through a box of paper a week is quietly moving a swimming pool through it every few months. And the recycled sheet in the same tray skips the tree entirely, which roughly halves the whole number.

So the email footers had a point. They just never mentioned it was about water.

Source: van Oel and Hoekstra (2012), the global water footprint study of paper.

#paper #office #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet #thewateryoucantsee

title: A strange fact from the water business: one of the worst things you can pour …
caption:
A strange fact from the water business: one of the worst things you can pour into a river is milk.

Not because milk is toxic. Because it's food. Water quality people measure dirt with a parameter called COD, the amount of oxygen it takes to break down whatever is in the water. Dirt gets eaten by microbes, microbes breathe oxygen, and that oxygen comes out of the same budget the fish are living on. Milk is so rich that its COD lands around 200,000 mg per litre. Raw sewage sits near 500. So when a milk tanker crashes near a stream, the cleanup crews arrive with the urgency most people would reserve for something glowing.

Once you have this number, the water world starts making sense. Discharge permits are written in COD. Treatment plants live and die by how much of it they remove. The textile effluent from the jeans post? A few thousand. A distillery's worst stream? Up to 100,000, which is why a brewery's treatment plant can be busier than a small city's.

Dirty, it turns out, is measurable. The scale is in the slides.

Source: Standard Methods (APHA); EU urban wastewater directive.

#water #wastewater #COD #watertreatment #thirstyplanet

title: Bread rarely makes anyone's list of thirsty foods, which is exactly why it be…
caption:
Bread rarely makes anyone's list of thirsty foods, which is exactly why it belongs here. A kilo of bread carries about 1,608 litres of water. Cut that loaf into slices and each one took roughly 65 litres, about the same as a seven minute shower.

Almost all of it is the wheat. Wheat is the largest crop on the planet by land area, a quiet carpet across Europe, the American plains, India, China and Russia. Around 70% of its water arrives as rain, which is the gentle kind. The concern sits in the other 30%. In parts of northern India and the Middle East, wheat runs on pumped groundwater, and the wells there have been dropping for decades. Same grain, very different sources.

Bread also makes the multiplication visible. One kilo is manageable. Humanity bakes hundreds of millions of tonnes of wheat into food every year, and every tonne carried its water with it.

Numbers in the slides.

Sources: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011); FAO.

#bread #food #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: A litre of milk takes about 1,020 litres of water to produce. As with steak a…
caption:
A litre of milk takes about 1,020 litres of water to produce. As with steak and eggs, the animal barely drinks any of it. The water is in the grass, hay and grain a dairy cow works through every day to keep giving milk.

The question this number always raises: what about the alternatives? Counted by irrigation water in one large global study, dairy is the heaviest option per litre. Almond milk comes next, mostly because almonds grow in dry places on pumped water. Oat and soy sit far below both. Different studies count differently, so exact figures move around, but the order stays fairly stable.

Worth adding before anyone clears out the fridge: per gram of protein, milk performs about as well as eggs, and much better than beef. And a carton from cows grazing rain fed pasture tells a different story than one from a dry region herd eating irrigated feed. The average hides a lot.

Numbers in the slides.

Sources: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011, 2012); Poore and Nemecek (2018) for the plant milk comparison.

#milk #food #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: The flush is the last most people ever see of their water. From there it star…
caption:
The flush is the last most people ever see of their water. From there it starts a trip that runs under every street in the city, powered mostly by gravity: the pipes are laid on a slight, carefully surveyed slope, all the way to a plant at the lowest point of town.

Two things about that plant surprise almost everyone. First, sewage is about 99.9% water. The entire system, the pipes, the tanks, the billions in infrastructure, exists to remove a fraction the size of a sugar cube in a bucket. Second, the plant runs on biology. The cleaning is done by tanks full of bacteria that eat the dirt, and the dirt they remove gets digested into biogas. The better plants power a large share of their own operations with it, which means your flush partly funds its own cleanup.

The number worth sitting with is global: by UN estimates more than 80% of the world's wastewater still returns to nature with no treatment at all. The technology is a century old. Most of humanity just doesn't have the plant yet.

Once you know the journey, the manhole covers on your street get slightly more interesting.

#water #wastewater #watertreatment #thirstyplanet

title: Next to almost every serious factory in the world there's a building most peo…
caption:
Next to almost every serious factory in the world there's a building most people never notice. Tanks, pipes, a smell of earth, a low hum. That building decides whether the river next door stays alive.

It's called an ETP, an effluent treatment plant, and the nickname inside the industry is the factory's kidney. Used water comes in carrying dye, oil, starch, salt, whatever the factory does for a living. The plant takes it out. The surprising part is how: the core of nearly every ETP is a giant tank of bacteria that eat pollution as food. Operators feed them, keep them warm, and pump air into the water around the clock so they can breathe. More than half the plant's power bill is just that, air for the microbes.

Which points at the real weakness. An ETP costs money every hour it runs, and it makes nothing anyone can sell. So in places with thin margins and thinner enforcement, plants get switched off between inspections. The technology was solved decades ago. Running it, honestly, every day, is the part the world is still working on.

Once you know the word, you'll start noticing the buildings.

#water #wastewater #watertreatment #ETP #thirstyplanet

title: A flooded rice paddy looks like the crop must need to grow underwater. It doe…
caption:
A flooded rice paddy looks like the crop must need to grow underwater. It doesn't. Rice grows fine in moist soil. The water is there mostly as weed control: rice tolerates standing water and weeds drown in it. Farmers have used that trick for thousands of years because it works and needs no chemicals.

The cost of the trick is scale. Rice feeds about half the world every day, and growing one kilo takes around 2,500 litres of water. Across Asia's paddies that adds up to roughly a third of all the irrigation water used on Earth, more than any other crop.

The interesting part is happening on farms right now. A method called alternate wetting and drying, where paddies are allowed to dry out for a few days before being flooded again, cuts water use by about a quarter without losing yield. It's low tech, it's spreading, and it's one of the biggest single water savings available anywhere.

Numbers in the slides.

Sources: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011); International Rice Research Institute.

#rice #food #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: Every number posted here so far was spent before the product reached anyone. …
caption:
Every number posted here so far was spent before the product reached anyone. Coffee, 140 litres. A t-shirt, 2,700. A steak, 3,100. Jeans, 8,000. Read enough of those and it starts to feel like a personal accusation. It isn't one.

Those litres were used in fields and factories, and factory water in particular has a property that changes everything: it's concentrated. A mill's wastewater leaves through one pipe, and whatever flows through one pipe can be measured, treated and sent back into the process. With equipment that already exists, 70 to 90% of industrial wastewater can be recovered. Plants doing exactly this run every day, quietly, on every continent.

The reason it isn't standard everywhere is rarely technical. It's cost, and whether customers, regulators or neighbours are asking for it. Asking turns out to matter.

This is where the account goes from here: less "look how much water", more "look what can be done with it". The machines, the plants, the places already doing it.

Sources: Water Footprint Network; Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011); industrial reuse practice.

#water #wastewater #watertreatment #reuse #thirstyplanet

title: A 200 g steak carries about 3,100 litres of water, and nearly all of it was s…
caption:
A 200 g steak carries about 3,100 litres of water, and nearly all of it was spent before the animal ever drank.

Cattle eat for roughly three years before slaughter: grass, hay, grain. Growing all that feed takes water every season, and when those years of feed water are divided by the meat one animal yields, beef lands around 15,400 litres per kilo, the highest of the common meats. Actual drinking water is about 1% of the total.

The number changes a lot with how the animal was raised. Cattle on rain fed pasture mostly use rain that fell on grassland anyway. Cattle fed irrigated grain in a dry region draw on rivers and aquifers. Same steak on the plate, very different water story behind it.

Breakdown in the slides.

Source: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011).

#food #beef #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: A 100 g bar of chocolate takes about 1,700 litres of water to produce. Most p…
caption:
A 100 g bar of chocolate takes about 1,700 litres of water to produce. Most people read that number twice.

The explanation is mostly the tree. Cocoa grows in the wettest parts of Ghana, Ivory Coast and Indonesia, drinks rain all year, and at the end of a season a single tree yields only a few kilos of beans. Then it takes a lot of beans to make a little chocolate. So each bar ends up carrying years of accumulated rainfall in it, around 17,000 litres per kilo, which on paper is more than beef.

Worth knowing before drawing conclusions: about 98% of that water is rain that fell on tropical farmland anyway. Cocoa isn't draining rivers. Its actual problem is temperature. The belt where cocoa grows well keeps getting narrower as the climate warms, and the industry is already moving farms and breeding for heat because of it.

The breakdown is in the slides.

Source: Mekonnen and Hoekstra (2011), Water Footprint Network.

#chocolate #cocoa #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: Fashion withdraws 93 billion cubic metres of water a year. Almost all of it c…
caption:
Fashion withdraws 93 billion cubic metres of water a year. Almost all of it comes back, and that is the problem.

Textiles is not an industry that consumes much water. It is an industry that discharges it: hot, alkaline, loaded with salt and coloured by dye that never bonded to the fibre. Colour is the part people underestimate. It is not cosmetic. Dye blocks light from entering the water, which cuts photosynthesis, which drops the oxygen fish breathe. A coloured river is a suffocating river.

Cleaning the water is the part industry already knows how to do. A treatment plant followed by membranes can bring 70 to 90% of a mill's effluent back into the process. But treatment doesn't make the pollution disappear. It concentrates it, and that leaves two problems standing.

One is the concentrate, also called brine: the salty stream left behind by the membranes. The other is sludge, known as biosolids: everything the biological treatment pulled out of the water. For decades both were simply a cost, trucked away or evaporated. The interesting work now is recovery. Salts pulled back from brine and reused in the dyebath. Sludge turned into biogas, energy and nutrients instead of landfill. The goal is a mill where water, salt and even the dirt all have somewhere useful to go.

Sources: Ellen MacArthur Foundation, A New Textiles Economy (2017); published wet processing benchmarks.

#textile #wastewater #watertreatment #effluent #thirstyplanet

title: The CEO of Levi's once told an audience he hadn't washed his jeans in a year.…
caption:
The CEO of Levi's once told an audience he hadn't washed his jeans in a year. It sounded like a stunt. It was actually water policy.

His company had just finished one of the most detailed studies ever done on a single garment, and it found something unexpected: nearly a quarter of all the water a pair of jeans uses in its lifetime is spent in the owner's washing machine. The farm grows the cotton, the mill dyes it blue, and then the biggest saving left on the table belongs to whoever wears them.

The full farm to shop number is about 8,000 litres per pair, and the slides show where it goes, including why indigo is such a thirsty colour.

One thread to pull next: all that blue rinse water doesn't just vanish. It goes somewhere, and that somewhere is one of the most interesting places in industry. Next post.

Sources: Water Footprint Network; Levi Strauss & Co lifecycle study, 2015.

#denim #fashion #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: There's a sea missing in Central Asia, and part of the reason is hanging in y…
caption:
There's a sea missing in Central Asia, and part of the reason is hanging in your wardrobe.

The Aral Sea was once the fourth largest lake on Earth. Then the rivers feeding it were redirected to irrigate cotton, and over a few decades most of it turned to desert. Fishing towns now sit a hundred kilometres from the water.

That's the uncomfortable magic of cotton: it's a natural fibre, it feels like the responsible choice, and it's also one of the thirstiest crops in farming. One t-shirt carries about 2,700 litres of water, roughly what one person drinks in three years.

The good news doesn't require shopping differently. It mostly requires keeping clothes longer. Every extra year a shirt stays in use, its water bill per wear shrinks.

The slides break down where the 2,700 litres go.

Source: Water Footprint Network.

#fashion #cotton #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: There's a number hiding in your morning routine, and it isn't the price.
caption:
There's a number hiding in your morning routine, and it isn't the price.

By the time a cup of coffee reaches a kitchen, about 140 litres of water have already been used to make it. Not in the kettle. On a hillside in Ethiopia, Brazil or Vietnam, months earlier, while the beans were still on the tree.

Here's the part most people never hear: that isn't automatically bad news. Most coffee grows on rain, and rain falling on a tropical hillside was never going to come out of anyone's tap. The story gets complicated only when thirsty crops are grown in dry places with pumped water. So the question worth asking about coffee isn't "how much water", it's "whose water, and from where".

That question works on almost everything you own. The slides show where the 140 litres actually go.

Source: Water Footprint Network: green, blue, and grey water.

#coffee #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: Somewhere in school, everyone saw that photo of Earth from space and heard "7…
caption:
Somewhere in school, everyone saw that photo of Earth from space and heard "70% of the planet is water." True, but it hides the real story.

The number that actually matters is 0.3%. That's the share of all Earth's water that people, farms and factories can realistically use. The rest is ocean, ice, or buried too deep to reach.

And here's the twist: that 0.3% never runs out. It rains back down every year. So why do cities go dry? Because water is the one resource that can't be shipped around the planet. Oil goes on a tanker. A river stays where it is. So one country has more than it knows what to do with, and another counts the days until the taps stop.

That's the story this account tells, one everyday object at a time. The full picture is in the slides.

Source: USGS Water Science School, Shiklomanov world water resources.

#water #hiddenwater #waterfootprint #thirstyplanet

title: Singapore has almost no natural freshwater. So it built a national supply out…
caption:
Singapore has almost no natural freshwater. So it built a national supply out of the water it had already used.

The country runs what it calls four national taps: rain caught across the island, water imported across the border, desalinated seawater, and NEWater, which is treated recycled wastewater that can meet up to 40% of national demand.

Here is the part worth remembering. NEWater is microfiltration, then reverse osmosis, then ultraviolet disinfection. None of that is exotic. It is standard equipment, used well and maintained properly. The engineering was never the hard part.

The hard part was asking people to drink it, and they solved that by showing the process instead of hiding it. A public visitor centre. Open data. Politicians drinking it on camera.

The barrier to water reuse is almost never technology. It is trust.

Source: PUB, Singapore’s national water agency.

#singapore #waterreuse #newater #watertreatment #thirstyplanet

title: Have you ever wondered how much water it takes to make a beer?
caption:
Have you ever wondered how much water it takes to make a beer?

Not the water in the glass. All of it: the barley in the field, the rain and irrigation months before the brewery, the brewing itself.

One 250 ml glass: about 74 litres. And almost none of it was spent at the brewery. The field grew your beer long before anyone brewed it.

The part I find genuinely hopeful: inside the brewery, making one litre of beer takes around four to five litres of water, and the best plants have pushed that below three. Brewing is one of the industries that measures its water hardest, because every litre saved is money.

Same story as your coffee. The water is real, it was just spent somewhere else.

Source: Water Footprint Network (green + blue + grey), roughly 298 litres per litre of beer.

#water #waterfootprint #hiddenwater #thirstyplanet #beer

title: “Bottled water is cleaner than tap.” It depends, but not for the reason most …
caption:
“Bottled water is cleaner than tap.” It depends, but not for the reason most people assume.

In most of Europe, tap water is held to a public health standard and monitored continuously across the network. Bottled water is held to a product standard and tested batch by batch. It is not required to be purer. It is required to be consistent.

Two things people get backwards. First, “natural mineral water” describes where it came from, not how safe it is, and it is legally allowed to keep minerals a treatment plant would remove. Second, the chlorine smell people dislike is not contamination. It is a residual, a deliberate trace of disinfectant that stops anything regrowing on the way to your tap. Bottled water has no residual, which is why an opened bottle left warm in a car is the worse container.

The honest nuance. Where the mains supply is unreliable, where a boil notice is in force, or where the plumbing is old, bottled genuinely is the safer call. Context decides it, not the packaging.

Got a water myth you want tested? Put it in the comments.
#water #mythbusting #tapwater #drinkingwater #thirstyplanet

title: Wastewater is not a dirty word, and it is not another word for sewage.
caption:
Wastewater is not a dirty word, and it is not another word for sewage.

It is any water that has already been used, by your shower, a brewery, a farm, and now carries something it did not carry before. Sewage is one kind of it. A factory's effluent is another. Rain that washed a street is a third.

Here is the part that surprises people. Typical municipal wastewater is about 99% plain water. The entire industry exists to deal with the last one percent. And that percent is enough, because bacteria in a river consume dissolved oxygen as they eat the organic matter in it. Fish suffocate long before the water ever looks dirty.

One word, wildly different problems.

#water #wastewater #plainwater #learnsomething #thirstyplanet

title: You drank about two litres of water today. You used more than ten thousand.
caption:
You drank about two litres of water today. You used more than ten thousand.

We call this the blue planet, but 97.5% of its water is salt. Of the little that is fresh, most sits frozen in glaciers or too deep underground to reach. What is actually available to eight billion people, every farm and every factory, is about 0.3%.

Agriculture takes about 70% of what we withdraw. Industry takes about 20%. That 20% is where I have spent my whole career, inside the factories and treatment plants most people never see. After all these years, the thing that still surprises me is how little any of us know about where water really goes.

That is why Thirsty Planet exists. Real numbers, one everyday thing at a time.

Sources: USGS Water Science School; FAO AQUASTAT; UN World Water Development Report.

#water #waterfootprint #sustainability #freshwater #thirstyplanet
